llm.summary: This Android automation skill is openly intended to control a connected phone, but it uses an insecure long-running Appium bridge with predictable /tmp command files that other local processes could abuse.

dimensions.detail: Launching Appium with --allow-insecure all and --relaxed-security is broader than necessary for a general automation helper and materially weakens Appium guardrails while the service can control a connected device.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill requires installing Python packages and using adb, uiautomator2, RapidOCR, and Appium; this is coherent with the stated function, but users should expect phone-side automation agents and local tooling to be installed or started.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The instructions disclose broad device-control commands, but the Appium fallback exposes many actions through a predictable file-based command interface and does not clearly scope use to a specific app, session, or user-confirmed operation.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: start_bridge.sh and bridge_daemon.py start background processes, keep an Appium session alive, write lock/command/response files in /tmp, and lack authentication or permission hardening for those IPC files.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: The purpose of reading screens, OCR, tapping, scrolling, typing, screenshots, clipboard input, and accessibility-tree access fits an Android automation bridge, but the capability is high-impact because it can interact with any app visible on a connected device, including sensitive payment or account screens.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Install only if you intentionally want a local agent to read and control a connected Android phone. Run it in a trusted single-user environment, stop Appium and the daemon when finished, avoid using it while sensitive apps are open, and prefer a version that removes relaxed Appium security flags and replaces predictable /tmp command files with private authenticated IPC.
llm.findings:
[AST4] expected: Use of subprocess to start Appium is expected for this bridge, but the verified --allow-insecure all and --relaxed-security flags make the execution surface overbroad.
[AST4] expected: Using adb pull for screenshots is expected, but ocr_bridge.py builds /tmp/{tag}.png from an unsanitized user-supplied tag, creating avoidable path-writing risk.
[TT2] expected: Passing Android SDK environment values into Appium is expected, but forwarding the full environment into a weakened Appium server increases unnecessary exposure.
[TT2] unexpected: The predictable /tmp/bridge_cmd and /tmp/bridge_resp IPC files are not necessary for the stated purpose without additional containment, and they allow local command injection or response tampering by other processes.
[SDI-4] unexpected: The insecure Appium flags were confirmed in start_bridge.sh and are not adequately justified or limited by the skill instructions.
[SQP-2] expected: Device taps, screenshots, OCR, JavaScript scrolling, and app activation match the automation purpose, but combining them with relaxed Appium security and persistent local control warrants review.
[RA2] expected: A background bridge is useful for faster automation, but nohup Appium plus a daemonized session extends the lifetime of a powerful local device-control endpoint.
